roadmap.title: How the path works
roadmap.intro: Every money plan follows the same 8 steps. These two people are made-up examples, not you. Switch between them to see how the path changes.

notReady.label: Not ready yet
notReady.summary: Example person: owes $2,400 on a credit card at 24.9% APR and has $300 saved.

ready.label: Ready
ready.summary: Example person: no high-interest debt, bills covered, and $1,000 saved for emergencies.

roadmap.detailHint: Pick any step to read what it means.

explain.notReady: The light is red because debt over 15% APR grows faster than investments usually do. Paying off a 24.9% card is like earning a sure 24.9%. Investing waits until the debt is gone. That's the smart order, not a failure.
explain.ready: The light is green. Bills are covered, there's no high-interest debt, and there's a $1,000 cushion. Now it makes sense to grow the cushion and start learning about investing.

milestones.title: Cover the basics
milestones.body: Rent, food, utilities and getting to work come first. A simple plan for where each dollar goes helps you see what's left.

milestones.title: Open a fee-free bank account
milestones.body: A free FDIC-insured bank or NCUA-insured credit union account keeps your money safe and stops check-cashing fees from eating your pay.

milestones.title: Save a $1,000 cushion
milestones.body: A small emergency fund means a flat tire or a doctor bill doesn't turn into new debt. Small, regular amounts get you there.

milestones.title: Get your job's 401(k) match
milestones.body: If your job adds money when you save for retirement, that's extra pay. Saving enough to get the full match is usually worth it.

milestones.title: Pay off high-interest debt
milestones.body: Debt over 15% APR, like most credit cards, grows fast. Paying it off is one of the surest ways to keep more of your money.

milestones.title: Grow your cushion to 3–6 months
milestones.body: A bigger cushion covers a job loss or slow months. Gig workers often aim for the higher end because pay goes up and down.

milestones.title: Invest for retirement
milestones.body: With a safe base in place, regular saving in an IRA or more in a 401(k) can grow for decades. This is money for later, not for bills.

milestones.title: Invest in a regular account
milestones.body: Once retirement saving is on track, a regular (taxable) investment account can help with other long-term goals.

questions.q: Do you have any debt over 15% APR?
questions.hint: This includes most credit cards, payday loans and title loans.

questions.q: Do you have at least $1,000 saved for emergencies?
questions.hint: Money you could use today without borrowing.

questions.q: Are your basic bills covered each month?
questions.hint: Rent, food, utilities and getting to work.

results.stopBills: Start with the basics. When your bills are covered each month, every other step gets easier. Free help: a nonprofit credit counselor or the CFPB guides on the Help page.
results.stopDebt: Pay down debt over 15% APR before investing. Every dollar you pay on a 24.9% card saves you about 25 cents a year. That beats what investing usually earns.
results.wait: You're close. Build a $1,000 cushion first so a surprise bill doesn't send you back into debt. Even $5 or $10 a week adds up.
results.go: Your base is safe. You're ready to learn how investing works. Start with the Learn page, then try a practice account before using real money.

andon.title: Life happened? Press pause.
andon.body: Lost hours, a medical bill, a family need. Pausing your plan is part of the plan. Stop adding money, keep your cushion, and pick up again when you can. No guilt.

grow.title: Savings calculator
grow.lead: See how a small amount each week could grow over time. Start with $5. That's Kaizen: tiny, steady steps.
grow.chartDesc: Lines show the balance each year at 4%, 6% and 8% growth, compared with the money you put in.
grow.gensIntro: Say you stop adding money and leave it alone. Here's how it could keep growing for your kids and grandkids, about 25 years each.
grow.inflation: These numbers don't include inflation, which means prices rising over time. Real growth is often lower. Investments can also lose value.
grow.how: We add your weekly amount for a full year (× 52), then grow the total once a year at 4%, 6% or 8%. For your kids and grandkids, we let the final amount keep growing for 25 more years each, with no new money added.
why: It builds the habit. The amount can grow later when your income does.
Time does most of the work. Starting small today often beats starting big later.
Gig pay goes up and down? Save $5 in slow weeks and more in good ones.

about.title: About this site
about.lead: Where You Want to Be is a free education project. It helps people who've been left out of money advice see a safe, clear order of steps, without shame and without sales pitches.
about.mission: In 2025, the typical White family held about $332,000 in wealth. The typical Black family held about $37,000. Many people are kept out by fees, jargon and apps that assume you already have money. We start where you are.
privacy: We don't collect anything about you.
No accounts, no cookies, no tracking, no ads.
The calculators run on your device. Numbers you type are never saved or sent anywhere.
The site loads nothing from other companies.
disclosure: This is education, not financial advice.
We don't recommend or sell any product, fund, stock or company.
We don't earn money from links. Outside links go only to free public and nonprofit resources.
For advice about your own situation, talk to a licensed professional. You can check anyone's license on FINRA BrokerCheck.
about.brokerCheck: Check a professional on FINRA BrokerCheck
about.ideas: We borrow three ideas from careful factory work: small steps (Kaizen), safety gates (Jidoka) and a pause button (Andon).

meta.title: Investing basics
meta.description: Index funds, single stocks and bond funds compared in plain words, with risk from 1 to 5 and yearly costs in dollars.

learn.title: Investing basics
learn.lead: Three common ways to invest, side by side. No products, no picks. Just what each one is, how risky it is, and what it costs.

cards.name: Index funds
cards.plain: One basket that holds small pieces of hundreds of companies.
points: Spreads your money across many companies, so one bad company can't sink it.
Goes up and down with the whole market. Best for money you won't need for 5+ years.

cards.name: Single stocks
cards.plain: A small piece of just one company.
cards.costNote: Usually no yearly fee. The real cost is risk.
points: If that one company does badly, your money can drop a lot, fast.
Hard to diversify with a small amount. Most beginners start with funds instead.

cards.name: Bond funds
cards.plain: A basket of loans to governments or companies that pay interest.
points: Usually moves up and down less than stocks.
Usually grows less than stocks over long periods. Often used to calm a mix down.

learn.feeCheck: A fund that charges 1% a year costs {high} on {amount}. A fund that charges 0.05% costs {low}. Same amount, 20 times the fee. Always check the expense ratio.
learn.beforeTitle: Before you invest any real money
before: Make sure your basics are covered, high-interest debt is paid down, and you have a $1,000 cushion.
Try a practice account first, so a drop doesn't scare you into selling.
Anyone giving you advice should be licensed. You can check for free.

meta.title: Practice a market drop
meta.description: Watch a pretend $1,000 drop 30% in a practice account, then read calm, step-by-step coaching. No real money.

practice.title: Practice a market drop
practice.lead: Markets go down sometimes. Feeling it once with pretend money makes it less scary with real money. Nothing here is real.
practice.afterDrop: Your pretend $1,000 is now $700. Take a breath. Here's what to know.

coach.title: This has happened before
coach.body: Big drops like this have happened many times. In the past, markets recovered over time, though sometimes it took years.

coach.title: Selling now locks in the loss
coach.body: Right now the $300 drop is only on paper. If you sell, it becomes real. Many people who panic-sell miss the recovery.

coach.title: Spreading out helps
coach.body: Owning many companies (diversification) means one bad company can't sink everything. Funds do this for you.

coach.title: Only invest money you can leave alone
coach.body: Money for rent, food or bills belongs in savings, not investments. Invest only what you won't need for 5 years or more.

practice.recovered: In this example, the balance slowly climbs back to {amount} over a few years. Real recoveries can be faster, slower, or not happen in the time you need.
practice.chartDesc: A line that starts at $1,000, falls to $700, and may climb back in the recovery example.
practice.what: A practice account uses fake money to buy and sell real investments at real prices. You can learn how it feels, with no risk. Some investing apps offer one for free. This page is a simple example, not a real account.

meta.title: My situation
meta.description: Money stories and steps for four situations: 50+ catch-up, gig work, first-generation earners, and moving from check cashers to a bank.

path.title: My situation
path.lead: Pick the one that sounds most like you. Each has a short story, a few steps that help, and a tool to try.
how: Pick the tab that fits you

catch-up.label: Age 50+ catch-up
catch-up.story: Sunita is 58 and manages a community services office. She wondered if starting now made sense. It does. From Day 1, the rules let people 50 and older save extra each year, and she has real years of work ahead.
steps: Keep your $1,000 cushion, and build toward 3–6 months. Don't put every spare dollar into retirement.
Pay off high-interest debt. That frees up money every month.
Use the extra catch-up amounts if you can, a little at a time.
Learn about Social Security timing. Waiting longer to claim usually means a bigger monthly check.
Talk to a licensed pro about taxes and your timeline.
facts: Extra you can add to a 401(k) at age 50+: $8,000 a year (2026).
Extra you can add to an IRA at age 50+: $1,100 a year (2026).
Ages 60–63 may be allowed to add even more to a 401(k). Ask your plan or a licensed pro.

gig.label: Gig and variable pay
gig.story: Tariq is 31 and drives and caters. Some weeks are great, some are slow. A fixed monthly plan never worked for him. Small, flexible steps do.
steps: Save $5 in slow weeks and more in good weeks. The habit matters more than the amount.
Build a bigger cushion, closer to 6 months, because pay goes up and down.
Set aside part of each payment for taxes. No one takes taxes out for you on 1099 work.
Get free tax help from IRS VITA if you qualify.
Practice a market drop before investing, so a dip doesn't scare you.
facts: $5 a week for 30 years at 6% could grow to about $20,555 (example, not a promise).
gig.tool: See how $5 a week can grow

first-gen.label: First-gen earner
first-gen.story: Ayanna is 24, the first in her family with an office job. She has a 24.9% credit card and a job that matches 401(k) savings. She wasn't sure which comes first.
steps: Cover the basics and save a $1,000 cushion.
Save enough to get your job's full 401(k) match. It's extra pay.
Then pay down the 24.9% card as fast as you can.
After that, grow your cushion and start investing for retirement.
Tap any underlined word on this site when something sounds confusing.
facts: A 24.9% APR costs about $249 a year for every $1,000 you owe.

banked.label: New to banking
banked.story: Guadalupe is 38, a home health aide and caregiver. She has used check-cashing stores for years because she didn't trust banks. The fees were eating her pay.
steps: Look for a free account at an FDIC-insured bank or an NCUA-insured credit union.
Ask about fees: monthly fees, overdraft fees and minimum balance rules.
Look for accounts with no overdraft fees. Some are made for people starting over.
Set up direct deposit so your pay goes straight in, for free.
Start a small cushion in the same place, even $5 a week.
facts: FDIC and NCUA insurance protect up to $250,000 per person, per bank, if the bank fails.
